paras: The threatened lynching of Joe Nebares took place in Waco, Texas, on March 24, 1888, when an excited mob gathered after Nebares, a barber, was jailed on an accusation of attempting to rape his ten-year-old stepdaughter. According to a Waco telegram, only the steel bars of his cell saved him from being lynched, and the Austin Weekly Statesman printed the story under the headline "Almost a Lynching." He remained in custody and was indicted by a grand jury within days.

Nebares, whose name the papers also spelled Nebroes and Nebraes, kept a barber shop on the square near the courthouse and had lived in Waco for many years. Dispatches called him "a Spaniard"; the Waco Daily Examiner first described him as an Italian and then printed a correction saying he was a Spaniard. His stepdaughter, named Birdie Nebroes in the telegram and Birdie Gros in the Examiner, attended the public schools and regularly brought him his dinner at the shop.

At about one o'clock on March 24, when the girl came to the shop with his dinner, Nebares was accused of attempting to assault her in a building behind the shop. The Examiner said that Policeman Mahau and several other witnesses came upon the two, and that Mahau arrested Nebares and placed him in jail. The telegram added that he was said to have been drinking that morning.

Word of the accusation "caused considerable excitement in the city," and an excited mob gathered. The telegram stated that "the steel bars of his cage only saved him being lynched," but it describes no attack on the jail, and the Examiner's account does not mention a mob.

The complaint was filed in Justice Makeig's court and referred to the grand jury, which took up the case on March 26. The Examiner reported on March 27 that the grand jury had indicted Nebares for an attempt to commit rape on Birdie Gros. No report of a trial or its outcome appears in the coverage.

The mob is known from a single Waco dispatch, which appeared as a special to the Fort Worth Daily Gazette on March 25 and, in nearly identical words, as a special telegram in the Austin Weekly Statesman on March 29. The Gazette's version called the act "one of the most heinous attempts at outrage ever known in the criminal annals of this county or the state" and reported the mob without comment, while the Statesman made the near-lynching its headline.

The local Waco Daily Examiner treated the case as a criminal matter, headlining the barber's nationality and declaring the circumstances "simply too horrible to be put on paper." Its later items concerned the correction of his nationality, with the note that no reflection was intended upon any nationality, and the indictment.

The papers differ on the spelling of the accused's name, on whether he was Spanish or Italian, and on the girl's surname, with the local Examiner giving Nebares and Gros and correcting itself to Spaniard.

accounts.label: Waco telegram (Gazette and Statesman)
accounts.gist: Nebroes/Nebraes was caught in the act and jailed, and an excited mob gathered; only the steel bars of his cage saved him from lynching.

accounts.label: Local paper (Waco Examiner)
accounts.gist: Policeman Mahau and other witnesses came upon Nebares and the girl, and he was jailed on a complaint in Justice Makeig's court; the paper mentions no mob and later reports his indictment.

framing.detail: The telegram called the act 'one of the most heinous attempts at outrage' in the state's annals and reported the mob without comment; the Statesman headlined it 'Almost a Lynching'.

The Waco Examiner headlined 'Italian Barber Assaults His Ten Year Old Step-Daughter', called the circumstances too horrible to print, omitted any mob, and two days later corrected his nationality to Spaniard.

conflicts.note: The local Examiner uses Nebares in three items; the telegram spellings vary even within the Gazette's text.
The Examiner itself corrected 'Italian' to Spaniard (A4).
The telegram says she went by her stepfather's name; the Examiner and the indictment use Gros.
